summary_md: Kamarthi, Vijayan, Wilder, Ravindran and Tambe (arXiv 2019, published AAMAS 2020) study influence maximization when the network itself is unknown and must be discovered by querying nodes. Starting from 5 random nodes, an agent gets 5 queries (each reveals a node's neighbours); greedy influence maximization then picks 10 seeds on the discovered subgraph, scored by independent-cascade spread (p = 0.1, 100 runs) on the full graph. Geometric-DQN, a deep Q-network built on a GCN plus DiffPool graph embedding and DeepWalk action embeddings, learns the query policy. Each policy is trained on 9 networks from four families (Indian villages, voles, retweets, homeless youth) and tested on 13 held-out networks from the same families. Against the CHANGE friendship-paradox baseline, the best variant per family improves by 7.91 to 26.6 percent of the gap between CHANGE and greedy-optimal (Table 4). The text quotes this range as 7-23 in some places and 7-26 in others. Reward scaling makes training on several graphs at once possible, and synthetic SBM graphs help. Inspecting the learned policy gives a simple heuristic, H2 (query the lowest-degree node among those just discovered), which beats CHANGE on several test networks. For Paul's systems, the main point is a boundary condition. The cosponsor graph is a fully observed public record. The recruitment and frontier code runs classic greedy on it and states that no ML is needed. The paper's learned policy only pays when edges are hidden. That premise fits the partially observed staffer graph, but only as a way to decide which directories or people to research next. It does not justify any reading of access or influence. The reported numbers pick the best variant per test set and give no confidence intervals.

bearings.paper_claim: The learned query policy exists only because the graph is unknown. Its own oracle (OPT) is greedy influence maximization on the observed graph, and rewards are scaled as (influence minus CHANGE) / (OPT minus CHANGE) (Eq. 1). Once the graph is known, greedy is the reference standard and the ceiling.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2 Problem description; Section 3.1 Rewards when using multiple graphs (Eq. 1); Section 4 Experiment setup
bearings.system_side: Budget-constrained recruitment runs classic cost-bounded max-coverage greedy over the fully loaded cosponsor edge-probability matrix PE. The code comment cites the (1-1/e) guarantee and says no ML is needed at this scale. Candidates are pruned to degree at least 0.1 x mean degree.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This holds only while the recruitment graph is fully observed (the 533-member cosponsor record). If the graph were a partial sample, the greedy-on-observed-graph result would be a lower bound, and a query policy could matter.

bearings.paper_claim: Discovery under a budget of T = 5 queries from 5 random seeds recovers enough structure that 10 greedy seeds reach 7.91 to 26.6 percent more of the CHANGE-to-OPT gap (best variant per family, 13 test networks, 4 families, IC p = 0.1, budget 10). Geometric-DQN discovers larger subgraphs than CHANGE, yet discovered-graph size does not correlate with influence score.
bearings.paper_location: Section 5 Results, Table 4; Section 6 Insights, Size of discovered graph
bearings.system_side: load_network reads the newest complete congress_cosponsor_network xlsx and mean-symmetrizes it. Every edge is treated as observed, with no model of missing ties. The component assumes cosponsorship is the influence and alignment tie.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's premise applies only if cosponsorship is treated as an incomplete sample of a latent contact network (informal ties, staff channels). For the published cosponsor record itself, there is nothing left to discover.

bearings.paper_claim: Every comparison uses a single-colour independent cascade with uniform p = 0.1, a budget of 10 seeds and the mean of 100 diffusion simulations, with no variance or confidence intervals reported. Tables 2 and 4 report the best Geometric-DQN variant per test network.
bearings.paper_location: Section 4 Experiment setup; Section 5 Results, Tables 2 and 4
bearings.system_side: The frontier runs a two-colour first-to-reach cascade. Its kernel is heterogeneous, p = x/(x+6) with partisan and susceptibility factors. Draws use edge-keyed splitmix CRN with MC 20. Seeds come from lazy greedy over a priority queue on the fully known kernel P.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Spread gains measured under uniform p = 0.1 single-colour IC do not carry over to the system's heterogeneous competitive kernel. Any reuse needs a rerun on the system's own P and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

bearings.paper_claim: A cheap learned or hand-derived query rule can prioritize which nodes to reveal under a fixed budget. H2 (query the minimum-degree node among those discovered in the last step) beats CHANGE on voles4 (72.8 vs 58.9), damascus (104.9 vs 95.2) and israel (34.2 vs 30.6). Queried nodes end up with higher true betweenness.
bearings.system_side: The staffer graph is assembled from partial directories and payroll. Outreach ordering is published PageRank, then route cost. The code says an incomplete search must not be treated as evidence that no route exists, so the code admits the graph is partially observed but has no budgeted acquisition policy.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies only as a data-collection prioritization (which offices or people to resolve next), judged on graph-completeness metrics. It must not be judged on spread, access or introduction probability (D-025). Influence language stays barred on revolving-door edges.

gaps_exposed: The cosponsor graph is treated as complete. No component models unobserved ties, or asks how far greedy recruitment and frontier results would move if part of the true contact network is missing from cosponsorship.

The staffer network is admittedly partial (incomplete searches) but has no budgeted policy for which directories or people to resolve next, and no metric for graph completeness after each acquisition round.

The system has not tested whether a cheap structural heuristic (for example H2-style low-degree frontier choice, or degree-ranked seeds) matches lazy greedy on its own kernel P. Such a comparison would show how much the MC-20 greedy machinery buys.
flags: Reported gains are optimistic. Tables 2 and 4 pick the best Geometric-DQN variant per test network or family, without saying how; no confidence intervals or seed-variance figures appear; and the range is given as 7-23 percent in the abstract and conclusion but 7-26 percent in Results. Quote it only as 7.91 to 26.6 percent of the CHANGE-to-OPT gap, best variant per family, 13 test networks in 4 families, IC p = 0.1, budget 10, T = 5 queries.
Pooled per-family averages (Table 4) span different network sizes. Quote them with the family label, never as one pooled figure.

Influence in this paper means simulated cascade spread. Carried over to the staffer graph, it must not become closeness, access or introduction probability (D-025), and influence language is barred on revolving-door edges.
The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). It makes no use of LDA, and it makes no reciprocity claim.
Metadata: the item file says 2019 (arXiv posting) while Paul's entry says AAMAS 2020. Both refer to the same work (arXiv:1907.11625v5).
paul_alignment: Paul's entry is a bare citation (Kamarthi et al. 2020, AAMAS Geometric-DQN, unknown networks) with no takeaways or system links, so there is nothing for the evidence to contradict. The note is not stale. The system as built has not adopted learned discovery policies: recruitment and the frontier run greedy on a fully observed cosponsor graph, and the template explicitly says no ML is needed. That fits the paper's own logic, where learning only pays when the graph is hidden. The open use is the partially observed staffer graph, framed as data acquisition rather than influence.

related.why: Same Tambe and Wilder group, also RL for influence maximization under uncertainty. That work handles uncertain seed take-up and is the source Paul maps to SGATE; Kamarthi handles an uncertain graph.
Same group's deep-RL approach to influence maximization, applied to complex rather than independent-cascade contagion.
Deep RL for influence maximization on graphs. It acts on edges in a closed network, where Kamarthi learns which nodes to query.
Uses graph embeddings and GNNs for influence maximization, the same representation machinery (DeepWalk, GCN) as Geometric-DQN.
Theoretical frame for sequential, observation-dependent query policies. It is the guarantee-based alternative to Kamarthi's learned query policy.
Compares cheap heuristics with greedy optimization. Kamarthi's distilled H2 heuristic, which beats CHANGE, is evidence on the same question in the unknown-graph setting.
Efficient greedy influence maximization under the same independent cascade model that Kamarthi uses as its oracle.
Competitive IC is the model behind the system's two-colour cascade. Kamarthi's single-colour IC results do not cover that rival setting.
